utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Stefan Waespi, Matthius Neuner, Daryl Mundis, and our case manager Andres Vatter. We will be joined during in the course of our arguments by our colleague Ms. Tecla Henry-Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And could we have the appearances for the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, lead counsel, and Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the appearances for the other Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and our legal assistant Nermin Mulalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would like to greet everyone present at this hearing in which we will be hearing the Prosecution's closing arguments. I would like to greet representatives of the Prosecution, who almost all are present. I should add that Ms. Benjamin will be joining us in the course of the morning. I would also like to greet the Defence lawyers who are present, as well as General Hadzihasanovic and Brigadier Kubura. I wouldn't like to forget anyone else in the courtroom, in particular the registrar who was of much assistance during our site visit. I would also like to greet the usher and the legal officer, the Chamber's legal officer. I would also like to greet the interpreters who are outside and the security officers. As I have already said, today we will be hearing the Prosecution's closing arguments. But before we hear these closing arguments, there is a minor issue I would like to raise which concerns the Defence's motion for an extension of the number of pages granted to them. The Defence stated that they had filed written submissions, a brief, of 200 -- consisting of 200 pages, but the directive said that it could only be 200 pages. So the Trial Chamber grants this motion, grants this additional number of pages, but I'll take advantage of this opportunity to inform both parties, the Prosecution and the Defence for General Hadzihasanovic of the following problem. According to the directive that concerns the length of briefs and motions dated the 5th of March, 2001, briefs and motions must be presented in A4 format and the margin on all sides must be two and a half centimetres. According to paragraph B of the directive, the size must be 12 points and there must be a two and a half line space between the lines. A page must consist of 300 words. Paragraph C says that final briefs should not exceed 200 pages or 60.000 words. In addition, the footnotes and quotes also included when calculating the number of pages and words. Similarly, paragraph C points out that a party has to request leave to exceed the limits set in this directive, and they must explain the exceptional circumstances that justify filing a lengthier brief. The purpose of this directive is to limit motions to a maximum of 200 pages and to no more than 60.000 words. The Trial Chamber has examined your written submissions and we drew the following conclusion. With regard to the Prosecution's final trial brief, it consists of 200 pages and there is nothing to say about that. However, we calculated that it consisted of 104.680 words, and having made the appropriate calculations, this would amount to 349 pages and not to 200 pages. As far as the Defence's pre-trial brief is concerned, in the case of General Hadzihasanovic, it consists of 202 pages but we granted additional pages. There were 114.230 words and this amounts to 380 normal pages. The Prosecution has therefore filed 149 additional pages and General Hadzihasanovic's Defence team has filed 180 additional pages. I would also like to point out that the size of the letters was 10.5 in the case of General Hadzihasanovic's Defence team and wasn't 12, which means that we have 340 pages. As far as Brigadier Kubura's Defence team is concerned, they only filed 75 pages and this corresponds to 25.000 words. There is nothing that I would like to add to that. The Chamber wanted to point this out. The Chamber did not issue this directive. The purpose of the directive is general and is applicable and must be respected before all Trial Chambers. So in future, I will -- I would like to ask both parties to bear in mind this directive. They should bear this in mind when filing or drafting motions and briefs. This is something the Trial Chamber wanted to draw your attention to. We will now go into private session. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now that we are in open session, as I said a minute ago, the Prosecution will be presenting its closing arguments today. Before we had our break, I said that the Prosecution intended to spend six hours on its closing arguments. General Hadzihasanovic's Defence team said they intended to spend six hours on their closing arguments, and Brigadier Kubura's Defence team will need four hours. We should naturally respect this schedule, and the Chamber's legal officer will calculate the time used to ensure that the schedule is respected because as you're well aware, we will be having a hearing on Friday afternoon in case we fail to complete our work on Friday morning. I'm now addressing both parties before we commence with the closing arguments, are there any other issues to raise? Mr. Mundis, are there any other issues you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as far as Brigadier's Kubura's Defence team is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, we have no issues to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In that case, Mr. Mundis, it is now 9.15, and time is now running for the six hours that you have coming. The hour-glass is running.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In order to save time, I will commence right with where our respectful submissions in closing this case will go. We will be using throughout the course of our closing arguments a number of PowerPoint presentations based completely on the evidence that Your Honours have heard during the course of these proceedings, which, as Your Honours are well aware, has run more than 220 trial days. We also, Mr. President, intend on using a demonstrative aid, that is a map which you will see before you, later this morning. We've shown this map to the Defence. It clearly is not a map that is in evidence, nor will we seek to have it in evidence, but at the appropriate time in our submissions later this morning, with your leave, Mr. President, I would ask Mr. Neuner to assist me in pointing out a number of those locations on that map which are based -- the markings on that map are based on material that is in fact in evidence. Let me begin by just giving a brief overview as to where our submissions will be going. As the Trial Chamber is well aware, and I'm sure my colleagues for the Defence as well, it's certainly impossible to discuss all of the evidence in a limited period of time. What we will be doing is highlighting a number of issues that we think are either particularly important or are issues which we would like to elaborate upon the material that was contained in our final trial brief. If you see on the screen before you, a rough outline, I will begin with an introduction, I will then address the Trial Chamber on the issue of the Mujahedin and the evidence which the Prosecution submits supports our contention that the Mujahedin were part of the 3rd Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. My colleague Mr. Waespi will then address the Trial Chamber on count 1 of the indictment, including Dusina, Miletici and Maline/Bikosi. My colleague Mr. Neuner will then address the Trial Chamber on the counts relating to Motel Sretno. And Ms. Henry-Benjamin will then address the Trial Chamber on Bugojno. We anticipate that those issues most likely will take us through the course of the today. Tomorrow morning in the time that will be remaining to us, Mr. Neuner will address, Guca Gora, Orasac and Vares. I should say time permitting we will address the Trial Chamber on the Zenica music school and some brief comments on the Bijela valley, but the latter two only if we in fact have time to do so. I will then address the Chamber tomorrow morning on repressive measures or failure to punish. We will then make some brief submissions with respect to sentencing and then conclude with some overarching concluding remarks. Again, we rely entirely upon our final trial brief which is certainly much more detailed than anything we will be addressing you during the course of the next day and a half, and again these comments are simply some either elaborations or highlights of particularly important points that the Prosecution would like Your Honours to consider in rendering the judgement in this case. I will begin with discussing a number of issues that have been raised in the Defence brief, and particularly the Defence brief of the accused General Hadzihasanovic. We will begin with some comments regarding the accomplishment of the mission and the mission itself. We will discuss a little bit about the role of discipline but before doing that, I would draw your attention to paragraph 68 of the Hadzihasanovic final trial brief, as well as paragraph 604 of the report of General Karavelic. In that paragraph, Your Honours will recall the Defence military expert stressed, and this is a quote now from the paragraph 68 of the final Hadzihasanovic trial brief: "The commander must avoid being drawn into using his resources to take on activities which, although may appear important and critical at any given moment, will distract him from his mission, if not prevent him from accomplishing the same." And there is a reference to paragraph 604 of the expert report of General Karavelic. The Prosecution would submit that to the extent that this paragraph is a reference to the duty of the accused to prevent or punish crimes committed by their subordinates, this is misplaced, for the reasons which we will be addressing in just a moment. Let's turn now to the relationship between discipline and mission accomplishment. Your Honours have heard a number of witnesses who were questioned about the importance of discipline and particularly how that concept relates to the accomplishment of a mission. For example, Sir Martin Garrod, General Garrod, was asked about the issue of discipline and agreed with the statement as put to him by the Defence that the issue of discipline is of paramount importance to any army and that it is what makes an army successful or an army that will be defeated. Similarly, General Reinhardt was asked about the role of discipline, and in response to a question with respect to good order and discipline within units of the army, indicated or testified that it's in the personal interest of the accused that law and order prevails because it is a key factor for the combat value of his forces. If his forces lose law and order, if they lose discipline, normally they become not such a combat-ready and trustful unit as he wants to have them. And it's much more difficult for him to execute his power over these subordinates. Why do we stress this, Mr. President, Your Honours? It's quite simple, because discipline in an armed force requires law enforcement. Again, Witness Garrod was asked a number of questions about the importance of the relationship between discipline and law enforcement. A commander must be sensible to the fact that army regulations will be respected, national law or common law crimes must be addressed, international law must be respected and action must be taken in the event international law is violated; and of course, he also agreed when the question was put to him by the Defence that the object of discipline is to make one's force operational and effective. This is not a concept that was alien to the accused, General Hadzihasanovic. I turn now to Prosecution Exhibit P284, which was a report of the 10th of August, 1993 concerning legality in the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the accused in that document wrote the following: "All these and other questions that relate to combat morale, combat readiness, order, discipline and legality, will be under continuous consideration at the command of this corps." Your Honours, we have heard on a number of occasions some of the difficulties that were encountered within the 3rd Corps in terms of meeting their mission. The Prosecution would submit to the extent that there were crimes which went unpunished within the 3rd Corps area of responsibility, that this failure to take the adequate steps contributed to the difficulties encountered by the accused in meeting the mission that was assigned to him. We've also heard, Your Honours, a number of witnesses testify and documents to the effect that orders were issued for units of the 3rd Corps to follow the law or to comply with the law. The Prosecution asserts that a commander must do more than simply issue orders that his subordinate units follow the law. A simple issue to follow the law is not enough. General Reinhardt was asked about the importance of follow-up when issues -- when issuing orders and testified as follows: "Issuing an order is not enough. You have to ensure afterwards that the order has been executed the way you want it executed." He was then asked a follow-on question, how do you ensure that an order has been executed the way you want it to be executed? And he testified that there must be a constant interrelation between the lower headquarters and the higher headquarters, and the ideal thing is that you give an order and the execution will follow your order the same way, and you don't have to interfere, but if necessary, you would interfere, and today you would interfere by giving written or oral orders by telephone, by radio, or what have you. Let me turn now to another set of arguments that have been raised on numerous occasions by the Defence, and we will categorise those, as the Defence has done, in terms of context. Your Honours, context is not always all that it appears. There have been several lines of arguments advanced by the Defence relating to context. For example, the ABiH was in a defensive posture in 1993. Well, General Reinhardt was asked about the effect of an army being in a defensive posture in terms of the duties of a commander to prevent or punish crimes, and his response was that a defensive posture has "No effect whatsoever. Whether you are in an offensive operation or defensive operation or retrograde operation, the law has to be applied no matter what you are doing in a military operation." Your Honours have also heard evidence led about crimes committed by either the HVO or the VRS, for example in Ahmici or Bandal [phoen] or Stupni Do, as well as the ethnic cleansing that was conducted in the Krajina, resulting in large numbers of refugees flooding into the 3rd Corps area. What is the effect of war crimes committed by the HVO or the VRS? Again, General Reinhardt was asked this question and his response is as follows: He told Your Honours: "If things happen on the other side, the more you are obliged to prevent things on your side. Otherwise, you come into a spiral of violence on either side where both sides basically are breaking the rules of international law which will affect your own soldiers in a very detrimental way." We've also heard, Your Honours, evidence, for example, that led by the constitutional expert, Trnka to the effect that the VRS and the HVO were illegal armies. Again, General Reinhardt was asked about the effect of that on the duty of commanders to prevent or punish crimes, and his testimony was again, it doesn't have any effect because no matter what the enemy is doing, the laws of your country are binding and obliging. So this doesn't have any effect on you as a commander of those Bosnian forces by that time. Let me turn now, Mr. President, Your Honours, to the issue of the Mujahedin. There has been a large amount of evidence presented on the Mujahedin by all the parties in the courtroom, but what I would like to do in terms of starting our discussion about the Mujahedin is return to the summer of 1992 when the Mujahedin first appeared in Central Bosnia and the testimony of Mr. Andrew Hogg, a reporter from The Times of London who, as you will recall, interviewed Ebu Abdel Aziz in August of 1992. Andrew Hogg testified that before Mr. Abdel Aziz permitted him to be interviewed, Mr. Hogg was required to get the permission from the Bosnian army. I will grant an interview if they allow it, Hogg testified, about what Abdel Aziz had told him. Andrew Hogg then went with an interpreter and obtained such permission, and where did he go? He testified that he went to "the army command post by the waterfall" in Travnik. Once Mr. Hogg had obtained that interview, or that permission, Abdel Aziz sat down and allowed Andrew Hogg to interview him. We are now going to play for you some excerpts from that interview. This is, of course, P112 and the transcript of that is P112 tab 2, I believe. This is the audio tape of Andrew Hogg interviewing Ebu Abdel Aziz. And the first questions and answers that we would like to play for you concern why the Mujahedin came to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: About killing the Muslims by the Serbians just because they are Muslims. Yes. So we according to that I came along checked the area. I found that it was the truth, that these Muslims are being killed just because they are Muslims not because they are Bosna or something else. Yeah. So I decided that our duty to defend these people. Yeah. Right. Do you expect the numbers here to equal the number of Muslims who went to Afghanistan to fight Jihad there? No no. There is no equal in it other than to my knowledge that very few Yugoslavian Muslims came out for fighting in Afghanistan. But this not a mathematical equalisation that you should help me so that I can help you. Yeah. No our duty is wherever Muslims been forced to leave the country or being killed or being punished because they are just Muslims because our duty I mean I or any other Mujahedin duty to help these people to defend themselves against any [inaudible] what do you call aggression they ... Yeah. ... they are getting from ... Right. ... from any people. Yeah. What has been the reception that you received from Izetbegovic and the Bosnian government? Did they welcome you with open arms or did it take a lot of negotiation to be able to ... No by, especially by Muslims yes, they opened their hands and their, we are welcomed and even they help us and any kind of they have of food or anything because they recognise that we are here to defend them. Right. To help them. Right. And we from the beginning from the first day we already announced that why we are here ... Right. ... that we are to help them and we go back to our country as soon as they feel, get peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The next questions, Mr. President, that we would -- or question and answer that we would play for you is again from the Hogg/Aziz interview, where did the Mujahedin come from? And Mr. Aziz also testified -- told Andrew Hogg where the Mujahedin had come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell me with regard to the soldiers to the Mujahedin you have brought well that have come here. Again. They are, with regard to the Mujahedin that are now here. These are people with battle experience I, I. These are people with battle experience. Yes. Can you give me an any idea where else they have fought? You mean from where they got their experience? Yeah. Most of them from Afghanistan but there are others from different countries. Even some of them this is the first time they are involving in Jihad. Can I ask about the claim that's made to us about Mujahedin which is that the Mujahedin do not fear death that you would regard it as a honour to die in battle defending Islam. Is that the view of the Mujahedin soldiers here? Mujahedin methods, Jihad methods, is either victory or death for Islam. It means Shada we call it Shada. Either victory or Shada. Shada means we being killed in battle for Islam. How do you spell Shada? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. S-h-a-d-a. Right. That means being killed in battle for Islam? Have you lost any soldiers? Yes. How many? From. One of the things I want to tell you that my people is they are not only from Arab countries. They are from Islamic countries. So they are, they are from different area even we have from England, from German, from Albania and other Arabic countries. So we lost about eight persons. When you say that your people are from England and Germany now are we talking about Muslims living in England ... Yes. ... Muslims living in Germany. They are English Muslim people or German Muslim people or Albanian Muslim people. Right. Then nationals of these countries ... Yeah. ... plus with eastern countries like Arabian or the Middle East or Pakistan or ... Africa. ... Africa yes, especially, especially for North Africa. Yeah. Right. But you've lost eight so far. You've been fighting for a month and already eight men have died. You've mentioned Pakistan, you've mentioned North Africa is it fair to say that there is a pretty large collection of people here from Egypt, Algeria, Tunisia? There are many, there are, I cannot count how many there, there are from each country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The next excerpt from this interview that we would like to play for Your Honours is a very brief one and concerns the support that the Mujahedin received from the Bosnians in the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Are you able to bring equipment with you? What the Bosnians from our point of view need desperately is weapons have you been able to help them in this? No this is the problem that we have here that because it is very difficult to bring any equipment and any weapons. Yeah. And the Bosnians themselves are providing us with the weapons we need which is not that big number and not heavy equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Finally, with respect to this interview, as Abdel Aziz informed Andrew Hogg, by August of 1992, he had suffered eight casualties. Hogg then asked him where the Mujahedin were active in terms of combat, and we will play for you now this excerpt from that interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yeah. Is this area basically from Visoko around to Paroba? This is the front on which you are fighting or have you people elsewhere as well? Yes this is the area it is starting from the border of the Sarajevo ... Yeah. ... until north to the ... there is no specific area we are fighting but different area. Right. One thing I want to tell you about my Mujahedin is we are under guidance or you can say control of Muslim forces. Yeah. Or something like that, call it. My Mujahedin and my rules or whatever you conditions is that we are not leader here. We don't like to have our own first line or our own base we working under their guidance and their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, when Andrew Hogg testified, he in fact made a couple of corrections to the transcript of the tape that you just heard, and he was specifically asked about a second change that he made, and he testified there is no such place as Paroba. When I asked the question, is this area basically from Visoko around to Paroba, he said: "It was something beginning with a K, but I couldn't make out precisely what, I'm afraid, on the tape." We would assert that that location is not Paroba but Karaula, which is in the area around the front lines, as we'll be describing to you in a few moments. At this point in time, Mr. President, we will move on to elaborate upon some of the instances which we have described in our final trial brief as involving joint combat with the Mujahedin, and we are now going to be talking about that section of our brief, and I anticipate I will remain on this subject through our first break. And at this point, Mr. President, with your leave I would ask if Mr. Neuner could sit, in effect, in the witness box and point out a number of locations that we have marked on the large demonstrative aid map that is before Your Honours. We also do have A3 sized copies of these maps. I've provided those to the Defence, but we do have copies for the Trial Chamber. We will move, Mr. President and Your Honours, in a chronological fashion beginning, just as Abdel Aziz did, with the summer of 1992 and the testimony of the witness Ibrakovic concerning an individual that he knew as Ebu Sahar who was killed in the beginning. The witness Ibrakovic testified he was killed in Visoko in 1992, in the summer of 1992, sometime in July or August. And you see the citation to that testimony. Again, this would be another example the Prosecution asserts of situations where Mujahedin who were involved in combat operations with either the TO initially but subsequently the ABiH in the 3rd Corps area and its immediate environs in terms of the mission that that corps had been given. In the autumn, moving towards the autumn of 1992, there was testimony about foreign fighters being involved in the area around Karaula. Two witnesses testified about this, both the witness Cuskic and the witness Merdan, Cuskic saying with respect to the Mujahedin, "The first time I heard about them was in 1992, perhaps when they participated in the Defence of Karaula. Perhaps a group of about 20 of them participated in the Defence." Merdan testified that in November of 1992, he heard rumours that in the Defence of Karaula, several foreigners had been observed defending Karaula from the Serb aggressor. In December 1992, as Your Honours are aware, there were a -- there was an operation in the area of Visoko concerning lifting of the siege of the city of Sarajevo. This was known as Operation Koverat. We will take a look first at a document which is P246. This is a document from General Halilovic, the chief of the Supreme Command staff. It was marked urgent, to be delivered immediately, and it was addressed to the 3rd Corps commander personally, this document dated 21 December 1992. And in this document, General Halilovic informs the accused Hadzihasanovic that the Koverta plan has been seriously jeopardised because of the shortage of men on the Buca-Paljevo axis. General Hadzihasanovic was ordered to find a way at all cost to send at least one battalion with 500 men from the 3rd Corps territory to that axis. I would now like to play for Your Honours an excerpt from Prosecution Exhibit P482 which runs about one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On the 29th of December, 1992, the second Visoko operation was carried out under the command of the Egyptian [unintelligible]. The Mujahedin moved from the front line Bijela Buca near Travnik to the mountains. These are the mountains that overlook the city of Ilijas, which is five kilometres away from Sarajevo. The mountains were liberated and the Mujahedin continued advancing until they reached some difficult territory. There was then an aerial attack carried out by the Serbs with the use of helicopters. The fighting continued from the morning until the time of the [intelligible] prayer. The enemy were defeated. Vast areas were liberated, and the city of Ilijas nearly fell into the hands of the Mujahedin. The Bosnian forces were not able to maintain the position gained, and the Arab brothers found themselves deserted in vast areas so they were forced to withdraw. A large number of the brothers were injured and seven of the foreign Mujahedin were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We would also refer Your Honours with respect to this clip and Operation Koverat to Prosecution Exhibit P514 and P513. Of course, P514 is the document that is signed by the commander of the 1st Company, Ramo Durmis, and we of course have discussed this document during the course of the trial, and Your Honours are familiar with P514 and 513. The next main instance where the Prosecution has alleged that the foreign fighters were fighting in conjunction with units of the 3rd Corps occurred of course in the village of Miletici on or about 24 April 1993. Mr. Waespi will be addressing Miletici later this morning. Shortly after Miletici, in fact at roughly the same time in -- the next day, there was combat operations on Mount Zmajevac, which is immediately to the west of Zenica, and Your Honours will note it is the high point directly above the Cajdras junction or the Cajdras checkpoint which numerous witnesses have testified about. The witness Alajbegovic was asked about operations on Mount Zmajevac, and although he said he personally didn't participate in this operation, Mr. Catic, along with soldiers of the 3rd Battalion were involved in that operation. If Your Honours then look at Prosecution Exhibit P462, this is a document which concerns a report on war booty after the successfully completed operation on Mount Zmajevac. Approximately two and a half weeks later, P558 contains the minutes of a 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade command meeting held with the Brigade Sura on 13 May 1993 at 1500 hours. And again the issue of war booty or distribution of war booty is on the agenda. Nihad Catic, whom the witness Alajbegovic had testified was involved in the operation on Mount Zmajevac, on or about 25 April 1993, at the meeting held on 13 May Nihad Catic apparently discussed the issue of war booty, and the minutes reflect the following: "The lack of organisation in collecting booty stemmed from our lack of experience. The Arabs did not permit access to one ammunition and explosives depot." Now, the Prosecution would assert that that indicates quite clearly that this 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade operation involved Arabs on Mount Zmajevac on or about 25 April 1993. This document goes on with respect to conclusions, under point 3, Adilovic is charged with holding talks with the Arabs about the war booty which they took. RP being the Bosnian abbreviation for war booty. In early June 1993, the Prosecution asserts that, again, foreign fighters were involved with units of the ABiH 3rd Corps in the operations around Maline, and again my colleague Mr. Waespi will be discussing in greater detail Maline/Bikosi later this morning. Let's turn now to Bijelo Bucje. There has obviously been a large amount of evidence that's been adduced at trial concerning Bijelo Bucje. Witness HF, for example, testified there were some in the Bijelo Bucje area, referring again to Mujahedin, because it was a very difficult part of the front line. They would go there on their own initiative and carry out some operations, he told us. But the Prosecution asks, Mr. President and Your Honours, did they really go there on their own initiative to carry out some operations? Let's take a look at Prosecution Exhibit P775. This is a report of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade to the 3rd Corps dated 20 June 1993, signed by the accused Kubura for the commander of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. This is during the period prior to his formal appointment as the de jure commander of the 7th but during the period in which the Prosecution asserts he was in fact the de facto commander of the 7th. And we have addressed that at some length in our final trial brief. But let's take a look at what the accused Kubura reported to the 3rd Corps in P775. The commander of the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade immediately sent a unit of 70 soldiers to the Bijelo Bucje sector, where this unit, along with others, contacted the command of the 3rd Battalion of the 17th Krajina Brigade. "A counter-attack was carried out from three directions, and the coordinated Ustasha Chetnik attack was repulsed and front line positions recaptured. During the action, four soldiers, foreign citizens, Arabs, were killed." He then goes on and says: "As well as three soldiers from the 312th Motorised Brigade and one soldier from the 3rd Battalion of the 17th." This language, Your Honours, suggests that the four soldiers mentioned, the four foreign citizens, the four Arabs, were part of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. Why? Because the language goes on to state: "Not only were these four soldiers killed but as well as soldiers from other units." But that's not all with respect to these operations in Bijelo Bucje area in mid- to late June 1993. We have the highly contested DH1360 which as Your Honours know has been or was revised, I believe at least twice. As revised by court Exhibit 5, DH1360 now reads: "Given that a relatively small unit, 30 soldiers, of Arabs, who remained behind when -- after the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade left this area, is operating autonomously in the Bijelo Bucje sector." Now, we know from the previous document, P775, that the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade was, in fact, engaged in combat operations in the Bijelo Bucje sector in mid- to late June 1993. We also know that when the 7th left that area, a relatively small unit of 30 Arab soldiers remained behind. The Prosecution would submit that they were, in fact, left behind by the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, perhaps to secure that area. DH1360 goes on to state, and this again is a report to the accused Hadzihasanovic on an inspection carried out on the 312th Motorised Brigade, it was recommended to the accused Hadzihasanovic that these -- this unit of 30 Arab soldiers who remained behind should be resubordinated to the 312th Motorised Brigade or pulled out of the 312th Motorised Brigade's zone of operations. And again we would submit the use of the term "resubordination" and not "subordination" is of great importance. Turning to the next area, we are talking now about the line between Mravinjac and Kamenjas as reflected again on the map which you have before you. Court Exhibit 13, which is the war diary of the operation group Bosanska Krajina contains an entry dated 24 June 1993 at 2100 hours, and it states, as set forth on the screen: "The Mravinjac, elevation 129, Suplja Stijena, Plane, Kamenjas, partially, line was seized." It then goes on to list what was reported as being seized in terms of war booty. One T55, which as the Trial Chamber is aware is a tank, an anti-aircraft machine-gun mounted on a TAM 150 truck. A number of anti-aircraft machine-guns, bulldozer, mortars and other light weapons. Turning to Prosecution Exhibit P790 an interim report dated 24 June from the commander of the OG Zapad, Selmo Cikotic, again to the 3rd Corps commander personally, Commander Cikotic reports on 24 June 1993: "Our forces took control of the territory, Mravinjac, Plane and Kamenjas. We have one killed foreigner from the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. We seized a tank, one anti-aircraft gun, and one anti-aircraft gun mounted on a truck." This corresponds with information contained in P598, which again Your Honours are well familiar with. I think it will come as no surprise to anyone that the Prosecution would be mentioning Ramo Abu Dzihad this morning and P598 relates to that individual. Ramo Abu Dzihad mentioned that the Arabs on Mravinjac captured a tank. The men of Novi Travnik captured a tank, seven anti-aircraft machine-guns and three anti-aircraft guns on Mravinjac but gave us nothing, he says. So we have information that the Arabs, we have evidence that the Arabs captured this equipment. We also have evidence reported by the commander of OG Zapad, Selmo Cikotic, that it was his forces who captured this material. The Prosecution asserts that this leads to the conclusion, again, that the Mravinjac-Kamenjas plane, along that axis, there was in fact joint combat between units of the 3rd Corps and more specifically of the OG Zapad and the foreign fighters in the last week of June 1993. Turning to the month of July 1993, in the area around Kacuni, we again have evidence of the presence of foreigners in and around active combat locations. P924, tab 4, which is an entry of the 3rd Corps war diary of 11 July at 1806 hours, and I point out this was formerly Prosecution Exhibit P604, at 1806 hours reports the following: "The 3rd Corps command received a report from the 333rd Mountain Brigade." This report concerned combat operations in Kacuni. It goes on to state that the HVO is swiftly digging in positions and their activities jeopardise an advance to Kacuni. "It will be difficult to regain control of the lost positions with the available forces. The Arab has been asked to solve this problem." Moreover, this report from the 333rd Brigade indicates that in addition to the involvement of the Arab, they are running out of ammunition. "They are trying to obtain some by purchase but they have no more foreign currency. They are asking for a certain amount of foreign currency for the purchase of weapons and ammunition." The next document related to this event in Kacuni or these events in Kacuni is P603. P603 is a document of the 3rd Corps commander addressed to the 333rd Mountain Brigade. The subject, approval for engagement of a unit. And there is a reference on this document, a reference to the same report that was reflected in P924, tab 4. That is, if you compare the entry at 1806 hours in the logbook, reference is made to the report received from the 333rd Mountain Brigade bearing reference number 0440942993. And you see the response or the letter, the document of the 3rd Corps commander going back, referring to that report which had been received from the 333rd Mountain Brigade. Again, P603 states: "With reference to your above document, our response is the following. We approve the use of this unit on the mentioned axis as previously agreed." But that's not where the document trail ends, Your Honours, because on 12 July 1993, as reflected in Prosecution Exhibit P434, the 3rd Corps commander submits a query to the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade command with an information copy to the 333rd Mountain Brigade. And in this document, the 3rd Corps commander reminds the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade command that engaged in your brigade there is a unit of 77 soldiers from the territory of Busovaca. It is the 3rd Company of the 3rd Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. Since the engagement of Arabs, who are ready to carry out combat activities in the 333rd Brigade zone of responsibility is conditional on joint combat together with your unit. The 3rd Corps commander wants to know if the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade has reserve forces that could be engaged in the 333rd Brigade's area of responsibility at their demand. This, we would assert, ties back to P924, tab 20 -- or tab 4, where the 333rd Brigade had reported that it will be difficult to regain control of the lost positions with the available forces. Let's move now into August of 1993 in the area around Petrovici and Misici. P477, a document dated the 9th of August 1993, addressed to the Supreme Command staff of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in this document, the 3rd Corps command, under the section 1.2, "Our forces, reports the following: The Muslim forces or Mujahedins brought from Travnik, as well as the part of Muslim forces from Zavidovici, which is also in the 3rd Corps area of responsibility, did not want to carry out an order. Why? Why didn't they want to carry out the order? Well, although thorough reconnaissance has been carried out with the aforementioned, and they did not show a single sign that they would refuse to carry out the assigned tasks, at 1900 hours, they had reported that they could not carry out combat activities by night. They could not carry out combat activities by night. We would respectfully submit that this is not necessarily a situation where the Mujahedin, for whatever reason, refused to carry out an order. They refused because, for whatever reason, they could not carry out combat activities by night. The 3rd Corps commander goes on and reports, "Due to recent behaviour of this group of Mujahedins from Travnik, they will be returned to where they have come from. The rest of the Muslim forces from the Zavidovici Municipal Staff I will probably disband and assign to the battalions of the 318th Mountain Brigade." Let's move on to Kruscica, September 1993, and again what the Prosecution asserts is that we have a pattern here, Your Honours, of consistent and regular use of foreign soldiers in combat roles by the 3rd Corps and its subordinate units. September 1993, Kruscica. Cuskic testified: "... at the beginning of September 1993, we did have a joint operation towards Vitez, the area of Kruscica, with a part of that El Mujahid detachment. Merdan: "... to the best of my recollection, it was in the beginning of September 1993. And to be even more precise, it was maybe the 5th or 6th of September 1993 when they were resubordinated to the OG Bosanska Krajina. And they were included, involved, in a combat activity in the area of Kruscica." Now, we've heard evidence, Your Honours, or the Defence have put forward evidence, that even after the formation of the El Mujahid unit they still weren't part of the army, and they still weren't carrying out orders, and they weren't under the effective command and control of the accused or the 3rd Corps. We submit, Your Honours, that that is simply not the case, and we will -- this example in September 1993 also reflects that. Again, C11 and C13, the operation group Bosanska Krajina logbook and war diary contains entries concerning the El Mujahid detachment on the 5th and 6th of September. The 306th Mountain Brigade war diary, C18, at 5 September 1993 at 1800 hours indicates that the 306th Mountain Brigade carried out an attack in coordination with the forces of the El Mujahid, 27th and 325th Brigades. Let's turn to the area around Grbavica, to the north-west of Vitez. Again, September 1993. The OG Bosanska Krajina logbook, C11, on an entry dated 6 September 1993 at 0230 hours indicates that a report had been received from the 325th Brigade and in this interim report, a large amassing of Ustashas was noticed. "They are probably preparing a counter-attack." Combat fatalities are listed including two killed and ten wounded from the El Mujahid unit. And with respect to that last phrase, "they are probably preparing a counter-attack," it's interesting to know some of the following entries in the logbooks and war diary of the OG Bosanska Krajina. Again, this entry is 6 September 1993 at 0230 hours. On 7 September 1993 at 1820 hours, the 325th Mountain Brigade commander sent a request to the OG Bosanska Krajina, "I ask that you urgently send me a company of Mujahedin for reinforcement until we repel the attack." Clearly the forces which they had seen massing the previous day had, in fact, come to pass. Two hours after, less than two hours after this urgent request for a company of Mujahedin for reinforcement, the following is contained in the Bosanska Krajina OG logbook. Sipic and Beba went to activate military police unit and Mujahedins as a help in the 325th Mountain Brigade area. So we clearly have an indication where the 325th was anticipating an attack, where they urgently requested a company of Mujahedin for reinforcement to repel the attack, and we see Sipic and Beba going to activate the Mujahedin in order to help the 325th Mountain Brigade. Again in September in the area, the greater area around Vitez Cuskic testified on the 18th of September 1993 there was a joint operation with the Mujahedin unit in the area around Vitez. In October 1993, we have evidence in the form of P618 that foreigners were involved in the area around Gornji Vakuf. And the OG Zapad, on the 9th of October, reports to the 3rd Corps commander in an extraordinary report and request. He asks for representatives or indicates in there "representatives of detachment El Mujahid visited me today and stated their readiness to engage a part of their unit in the activities in the area of Gornji Vakuf. It is conditioned with your orders. It's a fact that it should be done because any help in this area is welcome, even if it is more of a psychological character." Well, certainly we've had other evidence indicating the psychological character of an importance of the Mujahedin in this respect, and we would submit that that evidence is consistent with this request of the OG Zapad commander. Let's turn now to the area around Novi Travnik. Again, OG Bosanska Krajina logbook, 27 October 1993, at 1900 hours, under the heading, "308," indicating the 308th Brigade, the following is reported with respect to an attack carried out by the HVO on the Novi Travnik-Gornji Vakuf road. "The commander of the El Mujahid detachment was wounded and then a number of soldiers retreated." The 308th commander reported that he had four killed and 17 wounded and that the El Mujahid unit apparently suffered three killed and eight wounded. Moving into December 1993, again P495, a report to the Supreme Command staff from the 3rd Corps under paragraph 2.2, in the area around -- or indicating our forces, paragraph 2.2, in the areas around Dubravica and Tomica Gaj, the 3rd and 4th Battalions of the 17th Krajina Brigade, and the south TG, the 1st Battalion of the 7th, and the El Mujahid detachment put off the continuation of combat operations until tomorrow due to continuing reconnaissance activity. We would submit, Your Honours, that from the beginning of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. arrival of the Mujahedin in the summer of 1992, through at least the end of December 1993, there is clear evidence that the foreigners were involved in joint combat operations with units of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH, and we would like to offer you some concluding remarks with respect to this component of our case, and this testimony or this evidence comes from the so-called international witnesses, the witnesses from BritBat or UNPROFOR or the ECMM. And we would again, as we indicated earlier, Mr. President, we believe that these witnesses and their testimony is particularly important because they were neutral observers. They are -- they carry with them no bias. They were sent to monitor and observe. They are all trained professional military men and women. Their testimony, we believe, is of -- is of much weight and should be given such weight by the Trial Chamber. And let's focus on a few things that some of these witnesses said to us about the Mujahedin. And let's start with General Peter Williams from BritBat. He said: "I would say it was very difficult, I would say, impossible, for us to consider that there could be a well-armed, indeed well-motivated unit such as the 7th Muslim Brigade or indeed the Mujahedin operating within the 3rd Corps area with military capabilities that was not directly subordinate to the commander of the 3rd Corps. It would seem a very curious situation to have a heavily armed group of people wandering around inside your operational area without you having them, to some extent, to the greatest extent possible, under your command and control." He went on: "What I'm saying is that as and if and when they were in the 3rd Corps area, I cannot envision -- envisage them operating in that area other than under the direct control, albeit perhaps through the chain of command, but from the headquarters of the 3rd Corps." Mark Bower, another British officer, when asked about the Mujahedin, testified that: "What I mean is that where the Mujahedin 7 Muslim Brigade were, it is certainly where the fighting would be the most intense, and we could expect that that would be the prolonged main effort for the attack, that it is something which was, as I say, this combat indicator. It was of great importance that that's where this unit would be. It was -- it happened on a number of occasions, and it was too many occasions for it to be circumstance or coincidence, that wherever the main effort was, as part of the overall campaign within the six months we were there and witnessed the overall campaign, for it to be coincidence. It was too coordinated for this unit to just be in the right place at the right time on a battlefield, more than once or twice." We would submit that it wasn't coincidence, and the reason it wasn't coincidence was because the Mujahedin, as we've explained in a number of subsections in our final trial brief and highlighted for you this morning, these foreign fighters were integrated in and engaged in combat operations with the units of the 3rd Corps, and the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from this evidence that you have before you is that these foreign fighters were under the effective command and control of the accused Enver Hadzihasanovic, and with respect to the foreigners in the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, under the effective command and control of the accused Amir Kubura. I think, Your Honours, this would be an appropriate time for the first break.
