utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume, and I give the floor to the Prosecution to continue with the closing argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours. In the next hour or so I would like to address you on count 1 that relates to the crime base in Dusina, Miletici and Maline/Bikosi. But before doing that, I would like to spend the first part of my submission into the resources the accused had at their disposition. The resources to investigate, to punish the perpetrators, and I do that by showing what was done when normal crimes were committed, theft, murder, and we had seen mostly Defence witnesses, Judge Veseljek, Menkovic and Mujezinovic, who testified about the huge resources used for these crimes, and I'd like you to contrast it with what was done - and we submit almost zero - when it was about the killing of Croat civilians and soldiers who were captured. Let me start with Judge Veseljek who testified for the Defence and who told you what the effect of the inactivity to punish, to perpetrate crimes is. He was asked about that question and he said: "I fully agree with you that any event that is qualified as a crime should be investigated. Its perpetrator should be identified and punished." And he goes on the well-known concept to us criminal lawyers of general prevention. And he goes on and says that this concept also applies in times of war, and I quote: "General prevention in wartime doesn't only have an effect on potential perpetrators of crimes. It has a significance that is quite different. It also sends a message to potential victims. The message that if certain situations arise, they will be protected, and these potential victims can then take decisions as how they want to organise their lives." I believe that's a very, very important quote. It shows the impact of inactivity to investigate and punish criminals have on society as a whole. Now, the Prosecution submits that the accused Hadzihasanovic and Kubura could have made a difference. They could have sent a signal by investigating also and specifically into those three crimes we are talking about here, in my submission, Dusina, Miletici, Maline. Both accused were very well respected by their subordinates, by their superiors, by the internationals. There have been many quotes praising the accused. They had all the support they needed if they wanted to take action against the alleged perpetrators as they should have done and bring them to justice. Let me talk about the general picture that surrounds these investigations. Now, the Defence in their final brief, and I'm talking specifically about Defence of General Hadzihasanovic, made a big issue out of the circumstances and Senior Trial Attorney Mundis as alluded to that. If you look at paragraph 85 in the brief of Hadzihasanovic's counsel, they list all the problems which in their submission should have an impact on the abilities of General Hadzihasanovic to investigate. Pages 15 to 18 of the Defence brief talks about, I think, about 30 different problems, from the shortage of material, huge front line, the HVO checkpoints, which hindered the 3rd Corps troop movement. That's all fine. I don't think we dispute that. But in our submission, with all due respect, this had absolutely no impact on the ability of the accused to investigate into these crimes and punish the perpetrators. We had two international witnesses, General Reinhardt, our military expert, and I believe it was General Duncan, who talked about the battle, the situation of battle, which allowed both accused to devote time to the investigation. The first one is General Reinhardt, and he says here that, again there was no constant war, there was no constant campaign. The last sentence: "It was not a constant military battle one has to perceive here." And the consequence of that is seen on next answer he gives, and I quote him: "Besides that, the commanders who were very busy during the operation in executing and controlling the pursuit of the operations were capable of turning their attention to those things which they could not fulfil during the operations. And one of those things are their legal obligations, investigations and so on." So, yes, they had the chance to do that in those pauses I just mentioned. And similarly, General - I believe he was a general - Duncan, of BritBat, also talked about the fact that, and I quote him: "I would estimate there would be sufficient time for that on the basis that the action time is quite small compared with, if you like, recuperation time." And almost an anecdotal piece of evidence is his next comment, that there was apparently one of the features was that General Hadzihasanovic was warned, was advised, to yet introduce a 24-hour working staff organisation like the other corps had. I'm not saying they had a relaxed time but it appears they have sufficient time to complete, to fulfil, their legal obligations. Your Honours, a very important feature in investigating crimes in war times is the cooperation between MUP, the civilian police, and the military, and I would like to run you through a few pieces of evidence which show that they closely worked with each other, that especially the military -- the MUP acted upon requests, even orders, from the accused Hadzihasanovic. The first quote, Merdan, deputy commander of the 3rd Corps, alter ego to the accused Hadzihasanovic, and he says here, I believe it was in relation to Dusina: "Because they established full cooperation with the civilian bodies and with all the professional bodies that could establish what had happened to those people who were killed there," and he talked about his corps command. And he added that: "He received information that the civilian police would help with that. In other words, professional from the civilian police. Witness HF adds similar credence to this argument. Yes, there was good cooperation. Sometimes it was better, sometimes not so good, depending on the situation. We had joint actions with the MUP, that is, the military police and the security organ with the civilian police. We would always go together. And there was even evidence, and I believe it was from Witness Delalic, a Defence witness, who said on page 16372, when he was asked about the help a civilian police station could give to the 3rd Corps, and he said, and I quote here, I don't have it written: "They also protected civilians to the best of their ability. For a period of time, they were resubordinated to us because we didn't have enough strength in view of the breadth of the front line, so we were engaged on the front as well. They cooperated with us as far as they could, and as far as the combat operations allowed, and so on." So we have even a subordination of a civilian police station under the 3rd Corps unit, and I believe Delalic was the assistant commander for security for the 306th Brigade. Another quote comes from Menkovic, commander of a military police platoon, first the -- the first Bosanska Krajina Brigade and later he moved on to the 17th Krajina Brigade: "If somebody filed a direct report to the civilian police, and if they felt a need for our help or if they thought that the perpetrators were members of the military, then we cooperated and carried out certain parts of the investigation together." Another witness, Kapetanovic, just the last of the quote displayed for Your Honours: "And if the military police asked for such assistance, I know that they provided that assistance." And he talked about the civilian police helping out the military. Again, Witness HF, associated to the 3rd Corps, he talked about Maline. In the middle of the quote displayed in bold, I quote: "It was the responsibility and the duty of all the relevant organs to continue with the investigation until the perpetrators were caught. That activity never stops." And he goes on to talk about who assisted in this effort. His answer was: "The organs of the public security service and the MUP had the duty to continue. They worked on a parallel track with us. The military security, the military police, it was the duty of all of them." And at the end, he agreed that they all, the military, the civilian law enforcement, security, intelligence agencies, were all working together to identify the perpetrators. And we have legal bases for that, and that was Prosecution Exhibit 329, paragraph 50, where he talks about, again, the cooperation between the military and the civilian police. When the perpetrator or accomplice of a criminal offence, "Is a citizen of the republic who is not a member of the armed forces or a foreign citizen without diplomatic status." And we have a specific example of what could be the application of that law. Again Witness HF, on the specific -- on the specific example of that cooperation: "In another situation when a member of the humanitarian organisation Oda Nomad, I believe it was a British organisation, was killed by the Mujahedin, in that case we made an arrest together with the public security and detained the perpetrator in the KP Dom, pressed charges, et cetera." And Your Honours will note that was about a Mujahedin, the alleged perpetrator. The accused himself - and I'm talking about General Hadzihasanovic - made use of the MUP for investigation purposes - this is DH161/6 - when he directed an order to the command of OG Lasva. It was about ABiH members who illegally moved into abandoned houses from civilians. "OG, together with the bodies of the MUP, shall identify guilty persons who moved out Croats." That was his duty and that's what he implemented with his own resources and with the assistance of the MUP. The corps had all its abilities, also informal ones, to press for investigations when it mattered to them. This is Prosecution Exhibit 774, and it's a letter from the 3rd Corps command to the district military prosecutor, from the commander, from the command of the combat unit, to the military judicial authority, and it concerns a serious event; the death of 19 BiH soldiers and the wounding of others. And I quote the letter: "As the competent authority, after reviewing all of the material, you are to take measures to identify the individual who perpetrated this crime, as well as possibly other crimes. And to investigate criminal proceedings against him before the district military court in Zenica, which has jurisdiction in the matter." Let me turn, Your Honours, to investigation. What needs to be done if you are told, because it's your obligation, to investigate, to find out what happened? Mujezinovic, commander of the military police Battalion of the 3rd Corps, he said something obvious. What needs to be done if a crime happened? I quote him: "Well, if there is a crime, it is necessary to go and carry out an on-site investigation, to establish the factual situation and to detect the perpetrator of the crime." And what are the methods? We are all familiar with it, but it's important to see what it is. Mujezinovic, "The main method," and I quote him, "applied was to interview eye-witnesses, potential eye-witnesses or co-perpetrators, and this meant that it took sometime to collect all the evidence." Veseljek, he was more specific about what needs to be done, and I'll just guide you through a few of the attempts he made when he was sent out to the field to investigate crimes. And you remember he gave, I believe, testimony over two days and brought with him, triggered by the Defence, a large number of police reports and other military judicial documents which show what was done and indeed what they were capable of doing. He talked about DH278, and I believe I'll come to that in a moment. And he said: "In this particular case, whatever I was able to locate I collected. It was easy to collect evidence because the area was peaceful, it was secure, and I had ample time to collect all these things." And Judge Veseljek was talking about, and we'll come to that in a second, collecting forensics, something obvious, normal, mandatory, for every military policeman going to a scene. The first example I want to use to show what the police, military police, was capable of doing if they wanted, if they were directed, is P Exhibit 276 -- I'd like to correct the record. It's not P276, but DH276. It's a document dated 26 December 1992, called on-site investigation report. It's authored, signed by Judge Veseljek, the witness. And he talks about an event that happened the same day. That means they were capable, as they should, to show up at the crime scene the same date. On 26 of December 1992, they encountered a young man who was running around from a shop or something. Somebody wanted to stop him. So policemen chased him and they injured him while he was running away with shots. What happened was another example of cooperation. Immediately afterwards, the judge started carrying out the inspection, and shortly, the organs of the CSB and the military police arrived who secured the scene during the inspection. The judge, I have to add here, happened to be on the scene. That's why he called these other people. Now, what was done, and you see the title description of the scene, it was sketched and photographed in detail, and the sketch and the photographic documentation shall be a component part of the record. He went on, and you don't see it on this screen, that he collected cartridges, a gun cartridge was found there, and describes the calibre. Then later the judge left the taking of statements from the perpetrator and the witnesses to the military police organs and he adds when the on-site inspection was carried out. Also, eye-witnesses were listed in this very, very short report, two pages. Your Honours, that's one of the examples of what was done, just a normal day-to-day event, somebody running away allegedly from a crime scene. Let me take to the -- to a second example. This is DH276. And, again, we have the photography of the crime scene, then a description called "probable course of events," and you remember that was the example when one of the cows of an inhabitant was stolen. He called the military police and they came for the mere fact that a cow was stolen. Unfortunately, they couldn't arrest the perpetrators because they were shooting back. Cows were valuable at that time. So we have injured people on the scene. Now, the people from the military police who tried to arrest the perpetrators, the thieves of the cow, were named here. Data about the perpetrators. And then they concluded, after taking down all this information, that, and I quote: "It was found the military policeman acted according to service regulations in all matters and no measures were taken against them." That's a proper way to deal with a situation like that. State it down, see what happens, make an assessment, and put it on the record, not to hush it up as it was done in the cases we are talking about today. Your Honours, Judge Veseljek testified about a number of other documents and I listed them down here. Just a brief other document, and it's DH161, also listed on this slide, and in fact it's a letter from the accused Commander Enver Hadzihasanovic, who requested information in June 1993 about the theft of 1.5 litres of oil, a vehicle type Golf, and certain quantities of food, and he wants to have these allegations verified. This is the commander of the 3rd Corps. Another example, an interesting example, is DH1471, again a document that came with Judge Veseljek, and it's an official note by the military police battalion of the 3rd Corps, who looks into an aggressive behaviour by an alleged perpetrator. I'd like to read out what was said about the perpetrator. "He usually poses as a member of the MOS, Muslim armed forces." We heard about that. "And when robbing Croatian houses with owners who do not know him, he presents himself as a Mujahedin. He wears a long beard. This man is sought in order to be taken into custody and submitted for further proceedings. Victims and witness statements are being taken." Predrag Tomic. So they acted upon all these issues. Of interest here, even the military police talks about the MOS. And we heard evidence or witnesses from the Defence talked about that these forces did not exist. It's 1st October 1993. There are other instances, I can't go into all of them. DH155 talks about joint cooperation in checking vehicles. Joint cooperation, again MUP and the military police. DH1467, misappropriation of a video recorder and several medals and cups was also investigated, prosecuted by the 3rd Corps military police. After you have investigated, what do you do with the perpetrators? Mujezinovic, battalion commander, 3rd Corps, gave an example of how robust, aggressive, the authorities could be if they wanted, and they had to; that was their job. He gives an example when a formation of the green legion was suspected to be involved in criminal activities. And you know, Your Honours, how violent these instances can be in this environment. "It took us sometime for us to collect the documents and the material evidence, and of course with the security sector we submitted all this to the Prosecutor's office and when they accepted it as relevant on the basis of a plan, we did actually arrest and escort people to the Court." That was done when they wanted, according to their experiences, abilities, identify the perpetrators, collect evidence where they are, and make an action. I believe this refers to what they called action Golub, or pigeon. Another Judge, Your Honours, Judge Adamovic, also testified as to the risks an investigative judge took. He said, and I quote him on page 9492: "Even judges would go out very close to the front line. I remember a location that we went to where the opposing unit was literally 50 metres away from the trench where we were conducting an investigation." That was what was done when normal crimes were at stake. And the accused, Enver Hadzihasanovic, had a similar approach, as he should, in a communication to his superior command and to his fellow 1st Corps commander, when he said, and I quote: "We request that you deal with this matter more robustly as such actions jeopardise our units' lines of defence, since the aforementioned unit may not actually be in our area of responsibility but is next to it." P526, and it's about the abandonment of a position by one soldier. A serious issue, I agree; but look what was done, the commander of the corps sits down, writes a letter to his superior command, and to somebody he thinks could have more abilities to deal with it, his fellow corps commander. Coordination, horizontally. Witness HF states again the obvious. He asked one of his subordinates to "gather information about the event itself, about the perpetrators, about the circumstances, under which it all happened, all the relevant information normally sought in such situation." Witness HF at 17268. Brief on the involvement of the corps commander. Karavelic, the military expert from the Defence in his expert report, he says that: "All these investigations need to be done, possibly at the initiative of the corps commander, at least he's expected to ensure that it takes place." Your Honours, you heard a lot of testimony by internationals about the role of a commander, and we have all these quotes in our brief, and looking at the time, I don't want to spend too much on it but I urge you to follow these quotes - for instance, from Colonel Stewart - very, very closely, and give them due regard when you deliberate. But I'd like to quote a quote by Cordy-Simpson on command responsibility, when he was asked to comment about what another expert testified that command is a personal thing. And he said he would agree with it, and at the end he says: "Of course, things will go wrong. It's a subsequent action that a commander takes when things have gone wrong that is a test of whether he's a good commander or not." Not on paper but in reality, Your Honours. And the last two issues before going in detail to the crime scenes is a point the military expert Karavelic made on the reporting of collateral damage. He was asked about that and he said, and I quote the bold part: "If collateral damage, serious collateral damage, has been observed, the commanders of the units in the field have to report ... on the fact." It's not hushed up. It's being looked at. It's being reported. Battle casualty is no carte blanche, just raise it, nobody talks about it, nobody's asked question, it has at the minimum be reported, and Prosecution submits investigated, as they did, remember the example with the two military policemen who were doing some arguably legal action, it was looked into it, a report was made, and it wasn't followed. And lastly, Karavelic again on the powers of a corps commander: "Being a corps commander is a huge thing. Enver Hadzihasanovic was in charge of several thousand people with all the authority and responsibility that comes with it." Mr. Karavelic gave you an example of what he did when he thought two of his subordinate brigade commanders didn't live up to their duties. He fired them briefly. I quote: "I, as the corps commander, decided to remove them from their respective positions." And later: "And I instituted criminal proceedings against both of them with the military district court in Sarajevo." That's what the corps commander can do. He can use his military police. He has to use them. He can use the MUP. He can do action himself. He can even fire people as he should. Mr. President, Your Honours, I'd like to move on to the three specific crime scenes. And I don't want to spent too much time -- in fact no time at all, on the crime scene itself. We have heard Witness Ivica Kegelj, who testified that he personally witnessed the killing, the murder of the people who were captured alongside him. You have also heard another witness, Cvijanovic who testified live for the Prosecution about the death of Zvonko Rajic who was killed by Serif Patkovic, the commander of the 2nd Battalion. Now, there can be absolutely no doubt, although the Defence raised it several times, that there was no notice to the accused Hadzihasanovic, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that he knew about it. First of all, he was intimately involved, and you can see that in paragraph 120 of our brief. He was intimately involved in the Dusina operation. He signed reports, he ordered units, almost to the platoon level, and the military expert Karavelic acknowledged that. Now, as a result of this intimate knowledge, he knew about the casualties, about the killings. Just to mention Exhibit P132, the press release of the 3rd Corps. There is no way, in our submission, that the corps commander isn't aware of a public press release that went out on that day talking about the killing, the execution of Zvonko Rajic. But he did more than passively listening to information. He sent out two reports following the Dusina events. The first one is a report, and you see that on your screen, P237, where he talks about what happened in Dusina, and you see he takes note of the arrest of five to six HVO people. Second document, the famous meeting that happened the same day in Kiseljak. Several witnesses called by the Defence testified about that. And you remember that the HVO commander of the other side, the counterpart of General Hadzihasanovic talked about the exchange of -- that people who were exchanged were killed in Dusina. This provides clear notice. Witness Merdan, his deputy, came and testified in front of you, Your Honours, and said: "In fact, I talked to my commander about that meeting. " And he then, and you see that here, he informed the superior command of the events in Kiseljak, meaning what was talked about that meeting. Also, Totic, Your Honours, one of the HVO commanders in Zenica, and this is in footnote 548 in our brief. He said that he called Enver Hadzihasanovic the same night and talked to him about what happened. Now, especially Merdan committed himself and his commander and his unit on several instances to a full investigation into what happened in Dusina. And he did it in front of you, Your Honours. He said, and I quote him: "As I sat here today, I can say with full responsibility that the corps command did their utmost and went even beyond that, because they established full cooperation with the civilian bodies and with all the professional bodies that could establish what had happened to those people who were killed there." Very important, Your Honours, in our submission, is the fact that this was the first time that an army unit had committed a war crime. That is what Merdan testified. It wasn't the HVO crying wolf 500 times. Your Honours, it was the first time. So Hadzihasanovic had all reasons to take it serious. Stewart, Colonel Stewart, Bob Stewart, called by the Defence, told you that Merdan told him the people concerned in Dusina were going to be court-martialed. Merdan, he said, yes, he remembered that conversation as well. Now, the Defence tries to say that Merdan looked into the events overnight between the 26th and the later day, and came back to Stewart, to the internationals, and said, "We looked into it, we investigated it, battle casualties." So when the Defence asked Colonel Stewart, well, were you satisfied? Let's see what he says. "I couldn't understand why seven people would be killed. I thought it was probably the work of the Mujahedin. There would be no reason whatsoever for these sort of -- I just did -- didn't have time to investigate it but probably thought the BiH -- seven people killed? You know that's -- that's almost a deliberate attack. You know one or two people killed in a fire-fight, yes. Seven people, that looks to start like a massacre." Defence Witness Hadzic, called again to testify on Dusina, was talking about the hypothetical. And he said, again, if captured individuals would be killed, he would look into, as he should. Now, what did the accused and his military authority do? They could go, they had to go, to the crime scene, investigate, according to the standard set by their own witnesses. They didn't go. Nobody went to the crime scene in Dusina. The access was clear. HVO had gone on the control of the ABiH. Even the sanitary people from the civil protection went there. But no military police. They weren't interested in. Hadzic confirmed that. He said there were no subjective pieces of evidence in the case file. There were no witness statements or no information about possible witnesses either, and he even testified that one of the people killed was 70 years old. He didn't care. He said they wouldn't go there and make a proper investigation. And Your Honours, you have seen Ivica Kegelj who testified. He was detained at the KP Dom after the Dusina events for 13 days. Nobody questioned him about what he saw. He was an eye-witness, as was Franjo Krsto [phoen]. He was also there, although a shorter time. Of interest, Mr. President, Your Honours, is also the fact that Hadzic testified on pages 15116 to 17, that the investigative judge, this famous, infamous judge Strika played no role whatsoever. And he concludes, Mr. President, Your Honours, Mr. Hadzic, who was a prosecutor, who looked into the files, he said, an official investigation was never launched. These interviews which took place, allegedly, in the KP Dom, and we elaborate on that in footnote 571, were routine interviews, done with every captured HVO soldiers. They weren't directed focusing on the Dusina events because there was no investigation, as we heard. Witness Stewart was asked whether he was happy with the information provided about the investigation, so-called, into Dusina, and he said: "Yes, I would have liked that for every single crime committed I wanted to know what was going on. So the answer to the question is -- did I receive good information that somebody has been disciplined? The answer is no." And Your Honours, you may recall that in Dusina, not only Croats were killed, executed. There was also at least one of the ABiH soldiers, officers, and look what happened. Here they conduct a full investigation. They collect statements of eye-witnesses. They talk about detention and arrest of the alleged murderer, Cvijanovic. And this is Prosecution Exhibit P135. A clear indication again what they were capable of doing, if they only had wanted. Your Honours, there was no investigation; it was the opposite. The people, the alleged perpetrators were promoted. Serif Patkovic, commander of the 2nd Battalion, 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, 14th April, 1993, short time after these Dusina events, spread out through the valley to the internationals. He was given an award. Look at the first line of why he's given award. "Given the enthusiasm and results achieved in the struggle on Allah's path, the unselfish dedication in completing combat tasks," and so on. He gets another award and becomes even promoted later. This is P612, a proposal dated 17th August 1993. Proposal for the Golden Lily award, and you can read yourself, Your Honours, what the motivation for that was. And the same is true for the second named individual, perpetrator Vehid Subotic, also known as Geler. I think that means shrapnel also. P713 talks about the list of soldiers who were nominated for military medals. That was in May. And here it's signed by somebody we know, Serif Patkovic. Let me turn, Mr. President, to the next part. That's Miletici. Again, I don't want to spend time on the crime base of Miletici. You have heard evidence of people who were not eye-witnesses but who came to see the body after it had happened and testified that they saw the bodies, the way they looked like. One, I believe, had his hands tied behind his back, was sitting there dead. You also may recall that the people who were survived that attack on Miletici, the civilians, were led in a column down to Mehurici, Mehurici, a well-known place and you'll hear more today and tomorrow about this, where they were detained for a brief period and then released. There were Croat civilians but also three members of the ABiH. A negotiation took place between the local BiH commanders, I think from the 306th Brigade and the Mujahedin who were there, and the negotiations were successful. In our brief, paragraph 190, footnote 618, we will talk about these negotiations, especially also the people who played a big role, Ramadan, for instance. You see the references in our footnotes, the way he was, as we say, affiliated, with the ABiH army. Miletici, there was joint operation, joint combat, and my colleague Daryl Mundis talked about that this morning. This is again one of the examples of joint combat. You will see it in every single document, combat report. I listed here just three instances in combat reports and war diaries that clearly say that it was a joint operation happening not only on the 24th of April, 1993, but also on this place. I don't want to go over it. The Mujahedin are all over. They are acknowledged, they are taken into account, they are a factor. And that's reflected in these instances. Another information which shows to you, Your Honours, the presence and the involvement of these people, and also of the ABiH unit, is P664, by the command of the 306th Brigade, and there was an issue about the way these people were killed, and you can see the explanation given, a very detailed explanation, of what happened given very, very shortly after the incidents, by the commander of the 306th Brigade. He knows what's happening because he's involved. He has his eyes and ears there, where the Mujahedin are, his troops support them. It's joint combat. "With great effort and maximum involvement of people from the brigade we prevented even graver consequences of this incident." So they acknowledged they were there. They had influence to the very least over these Mujahedin and could change their behaviour. Just a few quotes from fact witnesses, Mr. President. You asked one of the witnesses, Pavlovic, about joint cooperation I might add over the objection of one of the Defence counsels, and I'm sure you recall the words what she said. She observed these people, the Mujahedin, and the ABiH together, approaching, and her opinion was: "I think that they did belong to the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They were with the Muslims." And I don't need to go further into the second quote. Another fact witness didn't testify live, P392, again talks about the joint action by both forces. Also of interest is a Defence witness. He was admitted as a Rule 92 bis. He was the assistants commander for security of the 1st Battalion of the 306th Brigade. He says, and I quote: "On 24th April, 1993, when most of the members of our battalion were in combat positions, we received a call from the duty officer who informed us that the Mujahedin had been in the village of Miletici and arrested one Croat and a number of Bosniaks from the village." Again, they had the capabilities, as they should, to look into what's happening in Miletici. They were interested what they doing, the Mujahedin, because they were part of their joint actions. My colleague, Mundis, already talked about the role of -- the observations by the internationals, here a quote by Witness Bower, which I don't want to elaborate upon. Very important, Mr. President, in those joint actions, are the locals. We already heard about the arrest of one of the locals who posed himself as a member of the MOS. Now, this piece, Mr. President, is P576, an HVO communication, so to speak, from the other side. And he talks about "the massacre in the village of Miletici was perpetrated by Mujahedins and local Muslims." It goes on: "Osman Tahirovic brought the Mujahedin into the village in a tractor. After that, the massacre happened." Your Honours, one of the significances of this document is that only three days after the event, the HVO, who had no access to the crime scene, apart from the representative of that UNPROFOR commission that went there to gather information. So the other side was able to get the names of the perpetrators within three days. Another letter dated almost a year later, specifically again names all these people, including Tahirovic. Very, very detailed. That's from the Busovaca police station, quite some distance from where it happened. Witnesses, Your Honours, were asked about these locals, and they knew them. Witness Ribo, for instance, was able to talk about Pasanovic, another local, and Jasarevic, one of the people named in the exhibit I just mentioned a moment ago. Tahirovic, one of the key anchors between the locals and the Mujahedin. Again, the witness Ribo was asked about him, and Ribo said "that he saw him cooperating with them," meaning the Mujahedin. One of the witnesses, Mr. President, talked about the mobilisation of soldiers. He was asked, but those who were older than 18, they were obliged to become members of the army, they had to be mobilised. His answer was: "Yes, yes, they fell under the obligation to be mobilised. That was pursuant to the decision of the Presidency proclaiming the state of, and it was the duty of every citizen of the state to defend their country." These people, Mr. President, these so-called locals, they were under clearly jurisdiction of the 3rd Corps, the military authorities, MUP, whatever. They could be Mujahedin as well, but certainly these local people could be questioned, interrogated, prosecuted for whatever they did. Nothing was done. They were left untouched, despite the fact that everybody knew who they were. And lastly, on this point, a quote from the UN report, Mazowiecki report on the former Yugoslavia, Payam Akhavan, who was a witness in the Blaskic case, he testified about a visit, I believe it was on 4th of May, to Miletici, and he later co-drafted a report, and let's see what he says. "The Miletici massacre was committed by," and I'll quote from the report, "members of government forces from neighbouring villages and Mujahedin." That's DH2097. That's a view from the internationals. And another interesting quote, an important point from Judge Veseljek, and I don't want to go into that, is that there was an obligation on everybody to inform about crimes. There are no cracks through which crimes go unpunished. The net is tight, Mr. President, Your Honours. And Witness HF, he talked about what kind of action he thought the 306th Mountain Brigade could instigate, and he talks about the possible perpetrators of Miletici, the Mujahedin, and he said they couldn't act on their own, but they could do so by approval of Witness HF, and you know what his position was. "I believe they would need to get approval from me because they were not members of the army." And he talks about Mujahedin. But they could do something if they only wanted. Briefly, Mr. President, on notice, again, there is no doubt that the accused received ample notice. This is P908, an HVO daily report sent, inter alia, to the 3rd Corps, the day after the incident. Five civilians were massacred in the village of Miletici. And a similar notice, little bit later, 7th May 1993, again talks about what happened in Miletici. And Your Honours, Witness Merdan told you that he went to the crime scene, the day, I believe, after the killings occurred in April. We have talked already, Mr. President, about the cooperation in general. Here again specifically on Miletici, Witness HF talked about that, and I quote: "In fact, I contacted with the head of the centre of the Public Security Service, Mr. Fazlic, who was responsible for the police in that area of responsibility. I also asked other services to provide me with any information they had about the event." Again, Mr. President, it's full cooperation from everybody available. And Witness HF again about steps and duties to investigate, and he talks about Miletici, quote in the middle: "It was the responsibility and the duty of all the relevant organs to continue with the investigation until the perpetrators are caught. That activity never stops." And he goes on a little bit more detailed, and the quote, I'm not sure whether it's in our final brief, is at page 17268: "The organs of the Public Security Service and the MUP had the duty to continue. They worked on a parallel track with us. The military security, the military police, it was the duty of all of them." And two final pieces of evidence on Miletici. First of all, again, Witness Akhavan from the Mazowiecki report. People, he said that -- and he was in Miletici; you remember, Mr. President. And I quote him: "None of the parties had engaged in any form of investigation, let alone prosecution of those responsible." And to counter one of the Defence arguments that, well, the national people looked into that. No, it was the job of the local commanders. And that's exactly what the meaning, the opinion was, of the special rapporteur. He expected all the parties to "bring to justice the perpetrators of such atrocities as are outlined in this report." In our brief we elaborated a little bit on that. The UNPROFOR commission certainly had no authoritative powers to summons people, to question them, to arrest them, to detain, to conduct forensic investigations. That was the job and the obligation of the resources the accused had at his position. Sipic, the commander of 306th Brigade, who was part, or I believe it was Zulic, who was part of the negotiations when the captured Muslims were released after being detained in Mehurici. He testified he was never interrogated. He was never asked to give an account, and he was a direct eye-witness to what occurred on the 24th of April, 1994. And lastly, Karavelic, on the impact Miletici had. "The event in Miletici, regardless of who had committed it, had the potential to exacerbate ethnic tensions in the area and possibly to lead to the failure of the cease-fire agreement." Again, Mr. President, the accused could have made a difference if he had properly investigated into this event, a big difference for the Lasva Valley. If I can take a moment, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to conclude my part of the oral submissions of the Prosecutor by briefly talking about Maline. And you know where the locations are. I believe that's one of the locations you visited the victims of that massacre. You're well aware of them. Again, the Maline/Bikosi massacre was initiated by a joint combat operation, as we have seen before many, many times, and we have of the witnesses, P92, who talks about that, and I quote her: "The BH army soldiers in Maline wore camouflage uniforms with their unit's insignia from which one could see that there were members of the 306th Mountain Brigade." That's what she saw. Most importantly, Witness HF, and again that may not be in our trial brief; it's in our closing brief. It's on page 17236 where he talks about when the Mujahedin would join in, and I quote him: "The Mujahedin would come, I don't know how, by information about combat, about combat activities, and they would come and join in those combat activities." And later: "But once the fighting started, they would join in the way they thought fit, and that is why they committed the crimes that we have referred to." And I believe in redirect the Defence counsel asked him at what time in a combat action they would join? Was it at the beginning, in the middle, at the end? And Witness HF said right at the beginning. Another telling example is P174, and that's a letter we'll come to in a moment again. That's a letter which was provoked by a letter by Mr. Mazowiecki. And here, from the 3rd Corps command, they talk about, and I quote: "Took part of" -- let me read out the whole quote. "Soldiers of the [illegible] and armed citizens, who were not members of the BH army units and who obtained weapons through some private channels, took part in the combat actions in the region of the village Maline." And Your Honours, if you look at the B/C/S version of this document, you can clearly see the number 306, where it says here "illegible." So I believe this is what the document says. Again, note, "Took part in the combat actions," a joint action. Then an important element again provided by Witness HF was about notice, that he had received notice, and he was -- you remember what his position was. He had received information about the killing of 20 people, and that they were executed by firing squad, and this -- that this crime had been committed by the Mujahedin, and that's an important point at this juncture. I'll come to that in a second. Another witness, Mr. President, Your Honours, who testified was Menzil. He was a doctor associated, I believe, with the 306th Brigade, the 1st Battalion. Now, he examined one of the survivors of this massacre, and he told you that he looked at it and it really didn't look to him like a battle casualty. And we can assume, and Prosecution suggests, you know, this was really part of an execution, and he was able to determine that by examining this victim. Of note, Mr. President, he was never asked to give an account of what he has seen, witnessed, himself, by anybody. Merdan again provides the notice anchor to the accused. He said that: "I suggested that we should go there in order to investigate what kind of murders or killings had taken place." Again, a clear commitment by the alter ego of the accused Hadzihasanovic to investigate. Now, Sipic, the I believe commander of the 306th. He now looked into that. He was present and he asked his assistant commander for security to investigate, and you can see that in the middle of this quote. And then it says they basically stopped the investigation, once they realised that it wasn't them. It wasn't the members of the 306th Brigade, although that was only the opinion of his assistant. Because later, and that's in the footnote 646 of our brief, it says: "It was only the assumption of the assistant for security that it was not done by members of the 306th Brigade." And then he goes on and says, and I quote: "I only asked them to inform the superior command that this has happened and that this was the Mujahedin who had done that." So that's it. There they stopped. Mujahedin, no more investigation. But remember this Mujahedin allegation so early, because it will change in the battle casualty in a moment. Witness F, again telling you about their abilities and indeed their commitment to look into information of the local Mujahedin, although nothing came out of it. "We made efforts to collect information about these local Mujahedin and we had some success." But then he goes on and basically says, you know, we couldn't really do anything. That's at page 17254. And I already told you, Your Honours, about the fact that Menzil was never interrogated by anybody about his firsthand account. Now, of interest, Mr. President and Your Honours, is the fact that in those days, in Maline, military police was available. Merdan visited, I believe, on the 12th of June, a few days later, Guca Gora nearby, and he had a military police escort; in fact, General Hadzihasanovic provided it to him. Why didn't they use that, the military police, to go to the crime scene in Maline where more than 20 people, civilians, captured HVO soldiers, were killed? That would have been the proper course of action. It wasn't done. To finish with the international reaction to Maline/Bikosi, because in October, it was picked up again, again by Mr. Mazowiecki and his expert group. He writes, and this is P120, a letter dated 15 October 1993. He writes, and I quote: "That on June 8, 1993, at least 25 Bosnian Croat civilians are reported to have been killed in the Maline village." And then later it says: "Eye-witnesses to the atrocities at Maline have claimed that so-called Mujahedin troops were involved, reportedly incorporated into the 7th Brigade of the ABiH." You remember, Your Honours, that this was exactly the explanation given by the commander of the 306th when he stopped his investigation. It was the Mujahedin troops. Now, two days later, 17th October, the Supreme Command now writes to the 3rd Corps and says: "Please give us information. We need to respond to Mr. Mazowiecki." And this is P171. Information whether massacre really occurred. Again, two days later, and you see, Mr. President, Your Honours, how quickly they could react when they wanted, at least formally, 19th October 1993, and this is DH 1498, the command of the 306th, who had Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. previously said it was the Mujahedin, now is forced to give an explanation. This time it's different. And I quote: "During a battle with units of the HVO in the villages of Maline, et cetera, the HVO suffered losses in manpower as a result of combat operations." And then at the end it says: "We repeat that all these individuals died in combat." Looks like a cover-up. A few months earlier they determined it was the Mujahedin or they had the opinion. Now it's since they have now to provide some details, they say, okay, battle casualty, for us no need to look into that. No explanation given whatsoever. Two days later, now the 3rd Corps command reports what they got from the 306th Brigade to the BH command and says, and you can see it at the bottom quote, and I quote from P174: "Since it was not a massacre, but the bodies of killed people by rifle bullets or shells, the perpetrators were not defined for objective reasons, as can be seen above." They even invent bullets or shells. The Mujahedin, Mr. President, Your Honours, have completely disappeared from this communication. So again, two days later, the 3rd Corps writes to the BH, and says, in reference to the request of Mr. Mazowiecki on the alleged massacres "we report as follows," and then the quote goes: "So nor was this a massacre of civilians as alleged in Mazowiecki's letter but an armed conflict in which, apart from RBH army members, the cited number of the HVO soldiers and armed civilians whom the soldiers had included in the fighting lost their lives." No proper investigation, nobody was interviewed, neither Sipic, all these people, the doctor. Just a bold statement, a complete cover-up, towards the international community. Let me end with the deputy of the accused Hadzihasanovic on the obligation of the ABiH vis-a-vis the citizens. "We, as the army, had to guarantee the safety of all the citizens, including the Croatian population." Nobody, not the accused and not Mr. Merdan, lived up to this commitment and to the legal obligations they had to investigate and punish the crimes that happened, occurred, in their area of responsibility. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, good afternoon, Your Honours. I will take you in a moment to Motel Sretno.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber would like to welcome Mrs. Benjamin. You may proceed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Given the advanced time I will continue, and I have prepared some slides which should help Your Honours to follow the presentation. I want to start my presentation on Sretno with a cease-fire agreed in Medjugorje. High-level negotiations had taken place, including Izetbegovic, Tudjman, Owen and Stoltenberg, and they led to a conclusion of agreement on the 18th of May, 1993 and an annex to that agreement said complete cease-fire and withdrawal of troops to the army barracks should be done by 1200 hours on the 19th of May, 1993. This provides a little bit the background of what has happened in Motel Sretno. Basically, what has happened, the Defence in their closing briefs, have accepted that the brigade military police of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade carried out arrests occurring and that members, and the Prosecution submits that these were not only members of the Brigade military police that day but also members of the guerrilla from the 2nd Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade who participated in the arrests. Why is that so? Because Witness Petrovic has testified that he was arrested on 18th of May, around 1200, 1230 hours, and I quote: "These two men had a wide green band around their heads, around the left arm. They also had a green band but it was narrower, and they were wearing camouflage uniforms." Another witness, Mr. Marusic, described his arresters. "These units were based in the motel. We called those units the Muslim armed forces or MOS would be the abbreviated form. They were in uniform. They had green headbands on them, and they had green bands on their arms, and on some of them these bands bore the inscription, 'the police.'" As this witness has observed, it was not on all of his arresters, bands or uniforms they were, that he could see the police inscription. Also, only three to four members of the military police from the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade had returned that day to Motel Sretno, and altogether 16 persons had been abducted, which is quite a lot, given that we had only three or four military policemen. So there were far more people involve in the arrests ensuing. And who were the victims? They were almost exclusively civilian. "Of those 16 of us who were detained, all of us were civilians except for one man who was wearing a uniform. He was a refugee in Kakanj, and I think that he was the only one who was a member of the Croatian Defence Council." That is what witness Petrovic testified to, Your Honours. And even the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade had information about the fact that the arrested persons were civilians. A document, P563, states: In the night of the 18th of May, 1993, the following, in Kakanj, our unit captured 16 Ustashas, civilians." Serious mistreatments followed that night, and I've put together only one quote as an example for the very many things which happened. It's from Mr. Bogeljic. And he says: "They put me on a chair there, and one of the men said that I would be hit 20 times with some sort of a wooden plank." I jump a little bit. "He said if I groaned, I would be hit 50 times. Then the first time I was hit, I fell back and hit my head on the stairs, and I think I lost consciousness for a moment. "Question: Do you recall what happened when you got back your consciousness? The answer is: "There was something warm on my face. I think one of them urinated on me. I still hadn't come to, not completely, you understand. It's difficult for me to think to all those events." Your Honours, the question is: Were the two accused present in the events surrounding the Motel Sretno incident? I will first deal with the presence of Mr. Hadzihasanovic. It is not alleged that he was present in the motel but during the arrest operation, one witness testified, Mr. Borovcanin, again the bandanas, he testifies: "They wore bandanas and some wore insignias on their arms and some had green bandanas around their heads. "Question: Could you continue. Tell us what transpired please? This group which was to my right stopped in a little meadow, in a little opening. I looked and I saw Mr. Hadzihasanovic who was talking to them." Mr. Borovcanin lived only three to four houses away from Mr. Hadzihasanovic at that point in time. He had seen Mr. Hadzihasanovic in a meadow, and the day afterwards, the following day, he saw on the property of Mr. Hadzihasanovic a table where he found a -- or where he saw a bag and a brief-case from an HVO commander. This also indicates -- who had been arrested. This also indicates that there was some relationship between the activities of the arresters, the people they arrested, and then the items which were found on them. I want to go back to the meadow where Mr. Hadzihasanovic was seen. What was the distance at the time? In examination-in-chief, Mr. Borovcanin said: "20 to 30 metres away from my house." When asked on cross-examination, 200 metres was suggested to him, and his answer was: "There is no 200 metres there. I'm sorry, it may be perhaps -- well, let's say not even 60 or 70 metres away. It's right nearby. 200 metres may be the distance up to the last house over there." I want to turn to Witness Izmirlic, who has referred to a book and said one can see the head of a man from a distance of 400 metres. This was taken from a book on military topography from Gvozden Colovic, DH1642, and I'm referring to page 6 here. If you look at the -- at the appendix there, it is confirmed a man's head can be seen at 400 metres and details on clothing on 100 metres. As stated, Mr. Hadzihasanovic was seen from a distance of 70 metres or less by a neighbour who had met him several times. Another indication about the presence or not presence of Mr. Hadzihasanovic is the Prosecution looked at the documents personally signed by Mr. Hadzihasanovic in the relevant time period, 18th and 19th May, and earlier. All documents in the period 18th until 20th of May are either type-signed by -- for Hadzihasanovic or signed by a substitute. So there is no personal signature. In the time period 16th until 21 May 1993, in evidence, there is only one document personally signed by Mr. Hadzihasanovic, and this is P276 dating 16th of May. It is displayed here. You can see the signature, and it was sent, it says here on the stamp, on the 16th of May. So there is no further indication that Mr. Hadzihasanovic had been in his headquarters, apart from this exhibit. What about the presence of Kubura? His unsworn statement, Mr. Kubura has said: "At that period of time, I was involved in combat operations 20 kilometres away from Kakanj." What is the substantiation of that claim? The unsworn statement of Mr. Kubura doesn't mention a specific location where he had been, does not mention a specific time frame, in what time frame he had been in that combat 20 kilometres away. Is there substantiation of that alibi in the closing brief for Mr. Kubura? It's paragraph 162. It just makes reference the two Defence witnesses have stated that Mr. Kubura was not in Kakanj at the time. It doesn't say positively where Mr. Kubura had been at the time or how long he had been there, at this other location. Also here, the Prosecution looked at the orders signed personally around the time period, and there is indeed one order on the 17th of May, 1993, P562. And as Your Honours can see, the date is 17th of May on the stamp here, and you see also the signature of Mr. Kubura, signing for Mr. Koricic at the time. It says relocate a part of the 17th Muslim Mountain Brigade command from the Bilmiste barracks to the broader village of Dusina. The question is who is meant with this order on the 17th with part of the 17th -- of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade command? There is an annex to that order which is displayed here, and the translation is here, and it says: "Plan of engagement of commanders of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade at the camp villages of Dusina from 18 to 21 May, 1993." If you look, Your Honours, which positions or which personnel was supposed to be in Dusina, you will find several persons -- or several positions listed here, but you will not find the Chief of Staff of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, and you will not find the commander of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade mentioned here. The question is: Where was the Chief of Staff? I'm referring -- on that day, on the 18th of May, 1993. I'm referring to P563, which states in the relevant part: "The unit is at full readiness and DNS Chief of Staff are in the 3rd Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. Written at 2300 hours on the 18th of May." Your Honours have heard where the 3rd Battalion was located at that point in time. It was the barracks was the Motel Sretno, and the question is who is meant by Chief of Staff? Were there Chief of Staff positions on battalion levels? In the 3rd Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, there was no Chief of Staff. The source for that is Witness Alajbegovic, transcript 18711, and Witness Kulovic, transcript 18815. They all denied that there would be a Chief of Staff in 3rd Battalion. Also in the other battalions, in 1993, there were no positions for Chief of Staffs foreseen. This is an inference drawn from P498 which lists on the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade command level a position of a Chief of Staff but not on the battalion level. So the interim combat report just shown places the accused Kubura at least from 2330 hours onwards on 18th May 1993 in Motel Sretno. The question is: How long did the beatings last? When did the beatings stop? And when were the persons released? And the Prosecution has listed the witnesses talking about this. Mr. Alajbegovic said it was on the following day, in the morning. More specific. Mr. Petrovic said between midnight and 1.00 a.m. on 19th of May 1993. Mr. Petrovic says after 3.00 a.m., about 3.30 or 4.00. Mr. Marusic states at 4.00 a.m. on 19th of May. On that day, on the 19th of May, Witness Bogeljic showed also his injuries at a meeting with the AB -- HVO chaired by a French UNPROFOR officer. And he states, transcript page 2127 to 2128, that his commander, Pavo Sljivic, has said during the meeting, he mentioned a name. When he was speaking he said Kubura, what are your men -- excuse me, I have to repeat that. He said, and I quote: "Kubura, look what your men are doing. And we are negotiating a truce and covering up our trenches." The arrest operation occurring in Motel Sretno had also earlier, Your Honours, heard evidence about this, arrests of military policemen from the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. The HVO had arrested them. If both arrest operations are compared with each other, one can see the disproportionate behaviour of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. The HVO had arrested nine military targets and one Iranian civilian, and evidence has been led that one ABiH detainee was beaten and released on the 18th of May 1993 while the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade had arrested 15 civilians and eventually one military target, and all of these 15 or 16 men were severely mistreated. Finally, I will deal with further notice to the accused Hadzihasanovic about the events on the 20th of May. Mr. Blaskic requested the joint Travnik ABiH command to visit and alleviate the situation in Kakanj, P682. It has been alleged in the Defence closing brief that the joint command was not operating or not convening meetings at that time. However, a close look at the documents in evidence show that even if no meetings supposedly -- even if no meetings would have occurred, both sides used the joint command as a kind of post-box to send messages to each other. And I'm referring here in the time period 17th until 23rd of May, to the HVO documents, DH1031, DH1040, DH1081. And the ABiH in turn also used this post-box, I will call it, for this purpose, this post-box, the joint command at that point -- that period of time. Your Honours, it's DH1032 and DH1045 until DH1048. These are messages which have been passed on by both sides. On 21 of May, 1993, there was a further protest letter sent to the 3rd Corps command. It's P684. And that particular letter, as Your Honours can see here, below on the screen the receiver is command of the BH army 3rd Corps in Zenica, and the relevant part makes reference to: "In the afternoon of the 18th May, BH army units led by the 7th Muslim Brigade from Zenica brought in 15 Croatian and Serbian civilians." And then goes on. It provides other examples of physical torture as well as psychological torture, so there is a clear indication that a crime has occurred. And finally, this protest contains a paragraph which reads, and I quote: "We request that the Muslim side conduct an investigation into the incidents in Kakanj and raise the question of personal responsibility." What were the measures? Mr. Kulovic, one of the persons who was in Motel Sretno around that time period, Mr. Waespi asked him: "Now, were you questioned by anybody, by your chief of security, by any authorities about this incident, about what you know or don't know about this incident?" Mr. Kulovic answers: "Nobody ever asked anything of me." This is the presentation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, good afternoon, Your Honours. Mr. President, as my colleague has indicated earlier, my task today is to address you on counts 3 and 4 of the Third Amended Indictment in so far as it relates to the town of Bugojno, in the municipality of Bugojno. Mr. President and Your Honours, the Prosecution submits that in mid-1993, the conflict between the ABiH and the HVO spread to the town of Bugojno, and in particular on the 24th of July, 1993 the 3rd Corps of the ABiH took control of the Bugojno town centre. Your lordships -- or Your Honours, in addition to all that my colleagues have submitted earlier, the ABiH soldiers of the 3rd Corps also established and operated a number of detention facilities in the small town of Bugojno in which many Bosnian POWs and civilians alike were confined and imprisoned. During the presentation of the Prosecution's case re Bugojno, the evidence reveals that the units primarily responsible for the conduct and running of these facilities were the military police units of the ABiH 3rd Corps OG Zapad and soldiers of the 307th Motorised Brigade of the operation group. In the indictment, the Prosecution has enumerated six locations where these facilities were established. And these are the gimnazija school building, the convent building, the Slavonija furniture store, the FC Iskra Stadium, the elementary school and the Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina building. Of note here, Your Honours, is that during the incarceration of the detainees, the relevant ABiH units above-mentioned transferred the detainees between the various detention facilities, moving them continuously from one detention facility to another. Your Honours, the Prosecution fielded several witnesses who testified on the appearance and physical conditions of these various detention facilities as it appeared during the conflict in mid-July 1993 and thereafter, together with the treatment endured at these facilities during the said period that they were confined. I wish now, Your Honours, to deal very briefly with each facility because I've been warned that I am on limited time. I in support -- I would use Sanction and some PowerPoint demonstrations. So we move to the gimnazija school. This facility -- and on our screen, we can see Prosecution Exhibit P58, which is the gimnazija building, and P64, which is a picture of the basement located in the building which was used for the facility. This facility as was state was located in the basement of the building. And all, each and every witness, who testified with respect to this facility described the conditions as terrible. Witness Mijo Marijanovic in particular, on day 33 at T 2744 to 2745, testified that the rooms located in the cellar of the building were about three-by-five metres long, holding 35 to 45 detainees, with the rooms being humid and hot, without light or ventilation. One witness testified the detainees were beaten until their bodies were black and blue. And still another witness, Vinko Zrno, had this to say, and I quote: "I remember very well the guy whose name was Mario Subasic. He was pushed down the stairs and fell on the floor, and at that moment I could see his eye falling out of the socket and he was bleeding all over his face." The major importance here, Your Honours, is that all witnesses, each and every one, said one main thing in common, and that was that all the detainees were subject to this -- to severe beatings at the hands of the soldiers of the ABiH 3rd Corps, the relevant units. Secondly, I would move on to the convent building. And the first exhibit, Prosecution Exhibit P56, shows us the building of the convent building; and the next one, Prosecution Exhibit P57, shows us a photograph of the basement of the building, which is where the facility was located. The units of the ABiH 3rd Corps guarding this detention centre was the 307th Motorised Brigade. The Trial Chamber heard witnesses testify that this facility operated somewhere between 24th of July 1993 to the beginning of August 1993 or thereabouts, and that the intake consisted of more than 70 Bosnian Croats, including POWs and civilians at any one given time. As was the case in the previously mentioned camps, the one previously mentioned by me and the other camps mentioned by my colleagues, Bugojno was no exception. Witness Ivo Mrso testified in depth about the mistreatment that occurred in the convent basement. And Vinko Zrno, on day 167, in his testimony, had this to say: He itemised the implements that were used in the beatings and this is what he said. "The rifle butt, boots, stones, police battalions [sic], everything, everything, they treated him like an animal, they were animals. The way they treated him was totally inhumane." One detainee who did not survive the beatings and who succumbed thereafter was Mario Zrno. Vinko Zrno, the deceased cousin, testified before the Trial Chamber on the said day 117 and had this to say, and I quote: "The two of us had been beaten at the same time. When I fainted, he would be beaten, and the other way around. After all the beatings, we were thrown together in a lorry. I was really in a bad shape. Mario was even in a worse shape. Perica Sistov took him in his lap. He tried to help him. Four or five minutes later, on the way back to the reception camp, Mario succumbed to his wounds. He died." The entire evidence, Your Honours, reveal that prisoners and detainees at the convent building suffered a similar fate as their counterparts in the gymnasium building, all done in contravention of the Geneva Conventions on the treatment of POWs and detainees. Mr. President, Your Honours, evidence was led through maps that showed that the detention facilities in Bugojno town were very close to each other. The Exhibit P65 shows the photo of the Slavonija furniture store; and P66 shows the basement of the building where this facility was operated. This facility, and in the interests of time, like the previously mentioned facilities, was guarded by units of the ABiH 3rd Corps, in particular the 307 Brigade. Evidence was lead by numerous witnesses on behalf of the Prosecution who testified that rooms in which detainees were held was always in constant darkness. The basement had no windows and the floors were covered in water, about ten to 15 centimetres high, constantly damp and cold. The Trial Chamber heard in evidence - and I think the Trial Chamber may have had the opportunity to see the furniture salon themselves - through Prosecution witnesses, the detainees were forced to sleep on pallets or on the concrete floors. And Witness ZE, a protected witness, described in detail and gave a comprehensive account of this facility and the conditions that they had to endure at this facility. Witness Alvir on day 31 testified, and I quote: "On that night," with respect to conditions, "on that night, we already thought that no one was going to be called out. It was one of the calmest nights until 3.00 or 4.00 a.m. in the morning. Then they called me out first. I went up. I was immediately hit as soon as I appeared on the ground floor. I think I was hit with some sort of a wooden stick. I fell on the floor because of the blow, and then they continued beating me with some sort of iron tubes. They were nickel, metal iron tubes, and this would make your skin break as soon as they hit you with these things. This went on for about half an hour or 45 minutes at least." At this facility, the witnesses testified that they were taken out nightly for beatings with various instruments, and Mijo Marijanovic in his testimony in day 33 describes same, and I quote: "Up in the shop, there was a sort of warehouse downstairs. They would take people up to the shop and they had various implements up there. They have those paper bags, various things. They would use whatever they could get on their hands. There were wooden implements, rods, iron rods, truncheons, police truncheons, various sorts of things." And when he was asked: "Did you get to know about these implements which were used for these beatings?" He said: "There was a toilet upstairs and when we passed by it we could see the weapons, the truncheons and the bags that they used." These physical assaults, your lordships, as recounted by witness after witness resulted in detainees suffering broken limbs and even loss of consciousness on many occasions and at least resulted in the death of one of the detainees, Mladen Havranek. Mr. President, the Exhibit on the screen, P62, shows the FC Iskra Stadium, the largest and perhaps the most notorious of the facilities. As with all the detention centres, the conditions here were deplorable and accommodation was inadequate. One striking feature of this facility is the detainees who were taken away from this facility for interrogation were never returned. Witness Mrso, in his testimony on day 1, testified before this Trial Chamber that he was advised to see the commander of the ABiH 307 Brigade to lodge his complaints about the deplorable conditions at the FC Iskra Stadium. The detainees at this facility all testified to the cruel, inhumane treatment that they endured at the hands of the ABiH 3rd Corps soldiers who were subordinated to the accused General Hadzihasanovic. Then we move on to the elementary school, and the Exhibit P60 on the screen shows us the school and P61 shows us the exact location where facility was. The sports hall in this school was in operation from July 31st to the end of September 1993. And again, this facility was guarded by the soldiers and military police of the ABiH 3rd Corps, OG Zapad. In addition to the deplorable conditions that we have heard the witnesses over and over testify to that were again customary to the detention centres in Bugojno for which I have already discussed, the facility which housed some 300 persons, including POWs and civilians, was always in constant darkness and the windows were permanently blocked and the ventilation inadequate. Ivan Mrso, on day 31, at page 2508, aptly described the scenario, and I quote, "as being lined up like sardines in a can." Even though the conditions here were deplorable, physical conditions appeared, according to the witnesses, to be a little better than the other facilities; but on the other hand, the pattern of physical abuse and torture that the detainees here endured was no different to any other of the detention facilities. Witness ZD, a protected witness, on day 35, transcript 2992, said that the detainees were singled out on a daily basis and beaten until late hours of the night. And on at least one occasion, there was evidence that demonstrated that one detainee was returned unconscious after the severe beatings. The Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina. A customary -- as customary, the witnesses brought to this facility were subordinated -- were subjected to the abuse and beatings as the other facilities previously mentioned. This facility too was operated during the period September 1993 to October 1993 or thereabouts, and most of the detainees who were surround HVO POWs who later became registered as missing after initially brought to the facility for questioning. Witness ZD went into detail explaining to us that each time a witness was taken out, or each time a detainee was taken out for questioning, no one knew where that detainee disappeared to after. Mr. President, Your Honours, I think I tried to condense the facilities and the conditions in the facilities in as limited time as I could have. I only have to go on notice, and if your lordships will allow me, I would like to finish. If not, I can continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. It's almost time to adjourn now. I believe that the Prosecution has another two and a half hours, but the Chamber's legal officer will make the necessary calculations and tomorrow I will inform you of the time remaining, because about three and a half hours have been used of the six hours allocated to you. Before we continue, there is another issue I would like to raise. Defence counsel informed the Chamber's legal officer that an artist would like to make some sketches of the courtroom and the Trial Chamber have a few questions about the matter. Mr. Bourgon, I'll give the floor to you because I understand that it is you who made this request.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In fact, yes, I've been informed of the fact that there is an artist who makes such sketches, and I asked this artist to make a sketch of the Defence as a souvenir. That's the only thing I would add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I have understood you correctly, the artist is outside the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've been told that this has been done on a number of occasions in other cases. All I would like to have is a sketch as a souvenir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The accused agree. They have nothing against the idea. Apparently not. As far as the Prosecution is concerned, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We have no objection, Mr. President. I do note I was in the lobby at the last recess, and the artist has indeed been sketching all of us based on what he observes on the large-screen monitor, and he's actually -- based on the resemblance he captured of me, he's quite good. There is not a lot to work with here but he is a very good artist, from what I saw. We have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In that case, the artist will continue to work as he deems fit. It's now quarter to 2.00. We will now adjourn and we will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. But first I would like to ask the registrar whether the hearing will be in this courtroom. Yes. In that case, we will continue in Courtroom II tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
